analysis.one_liner: Restores and expands Americans' ability to join member-owned credit unions while tightening their federal oversight.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the House 411-8 and the Senate 92-6, and the President signed it into law on August 7, 1998, after a court ruling had threatened to cut millions of people off from credit unions.
analysis.plain_summary: In early 1998, a court decision put federal credit unions that served multiple employer or community groups at risk of losing members. This bill responded by statute: it let existing members keep their accounts, made multiple-group credit unions legal, and opened a path for credit unions to serve underserved areas. To get the banking industry's opposition settled, it also imposed new rules on credit unions — independent audits for large ones, capital standards like banks face, and a cap on business lending — and ordered a Treasury study of credit unions' tax treatment.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit union members — ordinary savers and borrowers, especially people of modest means — keep their membership even where a court ruling would have forced them out [S7]. New groups can join credit unions as members of multiple-group and community credit unions, and credit unions may serve underserved neighborhoods lacking other banks [S7]. Consumers benefit because credit unions are member-owned nonprofits that typically charge less than banks [S7].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit union members and consumers of modest means

how_it_helps.text: Grandfathers every existing credit union member and every pre-enactment membership group, so no one is forced out by the court ruling Congress was responding to [S7].
Legalizes multiple common-bond credit unions alongside single-group and community charters, allowing a credit union to serve several employer or association groups [S3, S7].
Lets credit unions expand membership to include people in underserved local communities, neighborhoods, and rural districts that other depository institutions do not adequately serve [S7].
Reaffirms in law that insured credit unions have an affirmative obligation to meet the financial services needs of members of modest means [S3, S4].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and thrifts face more competition from newly expanded credit unions [S6, S7]. Credit unions absorb compliance costs: GAAP accounting standards, annual independent audits for those over $500 million in assets, prompt corrective action capital rules, and a statutory cap on business lending that forces some to shrink existing business loans within three years [S5, S6, S7]. Taxpayers bear the cost of credit unions' federal tax exemption, which the bill preserves while ordering a Treasury study of applying bank taxes to credit unions [S6, S7].
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks, credit unions' compliance costs, and the Treasury

drawbacks.text: The bill caps credit union member business lending at 1.75 times net worth and requires existing loans above the cap to be phased out within three years, reducing small business credit available from credit unions — a concession to banks that exempts only low-income-serving and business-lending credit unions [S5, S7].

New multiple common-bond groups are limited to fewer than 3,000 members unless regulators find an exception, and every expansion requires NCUA approval weighing harm to other institutions, so access gains are real but bounded [S7].

The bill orders Treasury to study applying federal tax laws to credit unions the same way they apply to banks — putting the tax exemption that funds credit unions' lower rates on the table for future debate, as banks sought [S5, S6, S7].
Credit unions' federal tax exemption means forgone federal revenue, which the bill's own findings acknowledge rests on credit unions' nonprofit mission [S7].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance a clear win for consumers: millions kept access to member-owned, often cheaper financial services, and underserved areas gained an entry route. The costs — compliance burdens and a business-lending cap — fall mostly on credit unions themselves, and the tax study hands banks an opening for a future fight without changing anything immediately. The bill is a compromise that traded modest regulatory concessions for a large consumer access victory.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 411-8, the Senate amended and passed it 92-6, the House accepted the Senate changes by voice vote, and the President signed it on August 7, 1998 [S9, S10, S14].

narrative.text: Introduced in March 1997 and referred to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee, which reported it amended in March 1998 [S1, S9].
The House passed it on April 1, 1998 under a suspension-of-the-rules vote requiring two-thirds, 411-8, with every voting Democrat and 213 of 225 Republicans in favor [S9, S10].
The Senate Banking Committee reported its own substitute version in May 1998 [S5, S9].

In July 1998 the Senate fought over bank-backed amendments: a motion to table Senator Gramm's amendment failed 44-50, with 49 of 55 Republicans wanting to keep it, before a modified version passed by voice vote; the Senate tabled the Hagel amendment 53-42 and the Shelby amendment 59-39 [S9, S11, S12, S13].
The Senate passed the amended bill 92-6 on July 28, 1998, with all 44 Democrats and 48 of 55 Republicans in favor [S14].
The House agreed to the Senate amendments by voice vote on August 4, and the President signed the bill on August 7, 1998, making it Public Law 105-219 [S9, S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit union members and the credit union movement came out ahead: the law preserved existing membership and legalized multiple-group credit unions, locking in their access route. Banks lost the main fight over credit union expansion but won tighter regulation of credit unions — audits, capital rules, a business lending cap, and a Treasury tax study [S5, S6, S7].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit union members and the credit union movement

sides.party_line_note: Passage was overwhelmingly bipartisan — 411-8 in the House with every voting Democrat in favor and 92-6 in the Senate — but the bank-backed Gramm amendment split sharply by party, with 49 of 55 Republicans voting to keep it and 41 of 45 Democrats voting to kill it [S10, S11, S14].

industries.note: The law legalized multi-group membership and grandfathered existing members, locking in credit unions' role as tax-exempt, member-owned lenders to people of modest means. In exchange, credit unions accepted bank-style audits, capital rules, and a business lending cap.

Banks face more competition from expanded credit unions that can now lawfully serve multiple employer groups and underserved areas. They salvaged tighter regulation of credit unions, a cap on credit union business lending, and a Treasury study of credit unions' tax exemption.

The law requires annual independent audits for credit unions over $500 million in assets and GAAP-based financial statements, creating new audit business. It raises compliance costs that credit unions may pass to members.
